posts.name: MindWanderer
posts.cooked:
Nice. Looks like one would run through a whole lot of index cards very quickly, so I'd probably use a whiteboard myself, but the benefit is clear.

However... It's more than a little video game-y. Telling the players what their objectives are supposed to be seems to me like railroading and detracts from the flow of a "role-playing" game. Players get to choose the means by which they achieve their goals but not what their goals should be. And it takes some of the discovery aspect away; players will be using their actions to try to check off boxes and not to learn and explore. (Of course, the constant march of the scene tracker does that, too; I'd be perpetually worried about "wasting" my actions in this system.)

What do y'all think?

posts.cooked:
I agree that the Scene Tracker is one big nitpick I'd personally come up with for the system, since as you say it feels like it would short circuit getting to just go with the flow. If I ever ran a Sentinels game I would be really tempted to just ignore the Tracker entirely and never use it as a result, as I honestly cannot see how my own group I'm used to playing with would ever in a million years be fast enough to fit much of anything at all into only 8-10 rounds.

So long as you use the Tracker, though, I don't see much of an issue letting the players know what's next on their agenda.

posts.name: speedyolrac
posts.cooked:
The Post cards are nice, Christopher and all the people who Demoed it at Pax Unplugged used them. They help focus the group, let them know what needs to get solved. And you can introduce them one as they find it. Remeber you are only giving the problem they can make use the solution, it is fun to see how players get to it.

 

Jeyse the screen tracker is also used to raise the stakes of the scene, the twists in each zone changes. It is also a way for heroes to use Yellow and red abilities without being in that zone. The scene tracker is there to speed up the game. If in 8 turns they do not finish it, you wrap it all up (Usually with not the best ending) and go to the next scene. I would give it a whirl before you change it. you can also add more time if you wish. I feel that 8 round is usually fast enough. I had to wrap up one game, but they just need to destroy the leftover bots, not really an issue.

posts.name: twoeyedjack
posts.cooked:
Sentinels RPG is a comic book role-playing game, intended to tell a fun comic book story. It’s not “a day in the life of a superhero”. Silver age comic books are short, sweet, and to the point. While you certainly could just give the players free reign to determine their objectives and their approach, it leads to long, drawn out sessions where the progress of the game is entirely in the hands of the players. Anyone with gamemaster experience knows how that will go; a lot of floundering around and putzing about until a bad guy is thrown in front of them, and then they punch the bad guy until it doesn’t get up again, and they steal the bad guy’s stuff.

Occasionally you’ll have a group that can stay on task, but those seem to be the exception and not the norm.

Railroad-ey? Yeah, I can see that. But in this system, that’s kind of the point. You’re not really trying to role-play a hero so much as you’re role-playing a group of writers for a comic book, role-playing as heroes in a brainstorming session to create an exciting comic book story. And to do that, the editor-in-chief (gamemaster) needs to keep the writers (players) on task.

Ultimately all a gamemaster for any role-playing game is doing is determining an end goal and putting up obstacles on the way to that end goal. Every session is going to have railroad tracks laid down, it’s just a matter of how good the gamemaster is at covering those tracks and making the players think they’re in control of the direction of the story. They really aren’t unless you put them in a sandbox world and let them run wild.

It’s been my experience, though, that while players say they want the freedom to do anything they want, when they actually have such freedom, they don’t know what to do with it. It’s overwhelming to them. They would rather have the gamemaster drop the hook right in their mouths but not look like they’re dropping the hook right in their mouths. They want to be taken for a ride but not look like the gamemaster is doing the driving. It’s all one big illusion. Lies upon lies, as the creators say.

Laying out the objectives in front of the players and then starting a timer gets players moving. It lights a fire under their butts and Spurs them to take action. How they tackle the objectives is what makes them a hero. If they walk away or say, Naw, that’s too railroad-ey," and want to do something else, then the action of the scene continues without them while their hero goes to a hotel and sits down for dinner. That’s not really exciting comic book story, and if that were to happen at my table then I pull that player aside and ask them why they are there. What do they hope to accomplish by not playing the game? Because if a player does that, then it’s a big sign to me that they don’t want to play or don’t like the game. If they aren’t interested, then that’s a waste of time and effort not just on their part, but on my part and the part of all the other players who are there who want to play. I have no problem cutting that player loose, because honestly, I have enough people around who want to play at my table that should one leave another will take their place. I’m lucky to have that option available to me.

I don’t think this is railroading at all, personally. I think it’s how the game is meant to be played. Superheroes need obstacles and objectives, at least when starting out. After they get the hang of how to be a hero, you could slowly transfer identifying objectives over to them, but that’s a learning process and not a first time playing strategy.

The end goal of the Sentinels RPG is to tell an exciting superhero comic book story. I think a gamemaster should keep that in mind constantly when running it. Superhero comic books don’t have pages or panels or ink to waste waiting around for the heroes to act. Readers don’t have time to read through four issues before something exciting happens. And it has been made clear that Sentinels is a Silver Age comic series, so there isn’t a lot of gritty realism or grey area dilemmas to ponder. It’s evil doers afoot and terrible plots that don’t make sense in the real world but for a comic book story it works. They’re exploring crossover stories and metaplots that span multiple issues and space travel that happens without real world science.

It seems that each session of Sentinels needs a sense of urgency to it. I can tell you from personal player experience that the index card element adds that sense of urgency and overwhelming odds while also keeping it clear what needs to be done to save the day. Don’t knock it until you try it.

posts.name: Jeysie
posts.cooked:
Well, ironically I don't have a problem with "railroading", in a sense, which is why I was totally bewildered and taken aback by twoeyedjack's lecture. I'm not out to flip off the GM's story, the goal of players should be to work with GM as much as the GM should work with the players.

Like, I have no problems with, for instance, the goals being "find and stop this signal", "beat up the robots", "save this person". I'd just like to have fun actually figuring out those goals in a way that makes sense to us and has a fun narrative, rather than feeling like we have to rush willy-nilly between everything with no real detail and making sure we get it all perfect the first time. That sort of extreme urgency isn't fun to me, it's just dull and stressful.

I mean I do appreciate that some people like the really simple dungeon crawl fight-fight-fight type of playing that's just "I swing my sword and roll dice", but I just don't find that interesting myself.

posts.name: NestorDRod
posts.cooked:
I got to go with Jeysie on this one. I derive my enjoyment of RPGs from actually playing a role, not from achieving goals and checking off achievements. One of the most memorable (and enjoyable) scenes in one campaign I was in involved the characters sitting and talking to each other wihtout a single die being rolled.

That is a personal taste, to be sure, and I'm in no way claiming it to be the "One Way to Play". But it is what I look for, and if a game doesn't support it, then I can easily shift to playing another game.

The impression I've gotten from the Starter Kit is that the Sentinels RPG hews closely to the card game not only in setting but in mechanics, i.e. a race to achieve objectives before time and resources run out. It feels to me like it focuses more on the "Game" than the "Roleplaying" in "RPG".

If that is what the designers are going for, I wish them the best of luck. I just may not be along for the ride.

posts.cooked: This is great!  One of the things I was most confused about was how to handle challenges.  Do I automatically tell the players what challenges are present, or do they have to discover them?  Do I tell them specifically what Overcomes have to be made or not?  If not the specifics, should they at least know how many Overcomes are required for a challenge or not?  Having never GMed before and only been a player in two RPG sessions, I had no idea how much information the GM was supposed to give upfront versus relying on the players to ask for it.  And since one of the groups I plan to GM for (my mom and brother) have never even played and aren't the most creative, I was worried they'd just be sitting there not knowing what to do.  Some groups might prefer things to be more open, having the players discover what they need to accomplish, but this videogame objective system is a lot more in my comfort zone.

posts.name: PlatinumWarlock
posts.cooked:
Correct me if I’m wrong, but you only really use the GYRO scene tracker when in an actin scene. During montage scenes – or general, open roleplay-- you don’t actually use that tracker.

To me, that’s where the real role-playing is done. Yes, you might ve some combat related tics or personality clashes during combat, but the argument that “I can’t roleplay while on a timer” seems to be a faulty one.

I do, however, liked keeping my players under pressure. I’m the sort of GM where, if you’re not prepared with your action when your turn comes around, I start visibly counting down. If I hit 0, the game moves on without your action. As such, i rather like the idea of “okay, you have 10 rounds to reinforce the bridge, save the civilians, and capture Citizen Moonbeam. Go!”

As a suggestion, instead of notecards? Try a Noteboard: https://thenoteboard.com
It’s cheap, reusable, and folds up for easy carrying. It’s easily one of the best convention tools I use while running games.

posts.name: rjc917
posts.cooked: As far as the Scene Tracker goes, I definitely see the value in it between both keeping the scene from going too long and being so tied in to the game's mechanics of allowing more extreme abilities and threats as the situation gets more dire.  But it also seems like it could definitely be a bit too constricting and will also likely be unbalanced for certain player counts.  A compromise I've thought of is to still have the scene escalate through GYRO, but not have a Scene Tracker actually visible to the players.  All they would know is what color the scene currently is.  The GM could still be using their own hidden Scene Tracker, or they could just be using their judgment on when to switch zones.  Either way would allow them to adjust to fit how the group is doing so they can keep the tension high, but not just make things impossible.  This also seems to make more sense thematically, because unless there's a bomb counting down or something, the heroes usually wouldn't know exactly how much time they have before things get really bad.  They shouldn't be going into a situation thinking "Ok team, we've got exactly 8 rounds to neutralize this threat."

Correct me if I'm wrong, but you only really use the GYRO scene tracker when in an actin scene. During montage scenes – or general, open roleplay-- you don't actually use that tracker.

Not always.

There's a lot of scenes where it's a mix of combat and non-combat stuff. So, the combat is pretty OK (although there often seems to be an impractically large number of enemies to deal with compared to turns available to take them down in), but then you get to this weird thing where you're somehow supposed to do in one or two Overcome checks something that really should have way more incremental steps if you're roleplaying it out in the sort of detail I'm used to, including the steps of your PC being able to gather the info needed to even know what to do in the first place.

Then there's stuff like the Tomb of Anubis scene, where you're supposed to go through like 8 rooms in 11 rounds when it feels like it should be that a properly fleshed out single room roleplaying-wise should take several "rounds" just on its own to go through.

And… this isn't me saying the adventures are designed poorly, because I actually think they look rather fun taken as a whole. It's just trying to imagine accomplishing all this in such a narrow window of time that's making me "meh", which is why I'm narrowing in on just that single problem rather than saying I dislike everything about it.

PlatinumWarlock:

I do, however, liked keeping my players under pressure. I'm the sort of GM where, if you're not prepared with your action when your turn comes around, I start visibly counting down. If I hit 0, the game moves on without your action. As such, i rather like the idea of "okay, you have 10 rounds to reinforce the bridge, save the civilians, and capture Citizen Moonbeam. Go!"

See, I feel you're making the exact same sort of mistake twoeyedjack is making in the discussion.

It's not "Oh gosh I'm not prepared with my action."

It's more like "Roleplaying this out in a natural, normal flow would take about five steps, all of which I'm prepared to progress with promptly whenever it's my turn to help progress them, but we apparently have to somehow condense all that down into one single step instead because the timer's ticking."

You folks also seem to acting like it's a question of single players bogging things down for everyone else when I'm trying to say that every person in my old group had pretty much a similar slower-paced style.

Like twoeyedjack is sitting there going "it leads to long, drawn out sessions where the progress of the game is entirely in the hands of the players" and my reaction was, "Yeah, everyone in my group including the GM loves that sort of thing! …er, oh wait, you're actually saying you hate that? Uh… well… now I'm confused?"

Like if the players in my old group caught on that they were under a timer, then we'd get bogged down in wanting to out-of-character debate everything we were going to do beforehand just so we wouldn't be caught unable to do everything in-character. It would drag out the pace of the game instead of speeding it up.

NestorDRod:

That is a personal taste, to be sure, and I'm in no way claiming it to be the "One Way to Play". But it is what I look for, and if a game doesn't support it, then I can easily shift to playing another game.

Yeah. But in this case I do feel like the system is like… 90% there? And does a lot of stuff I really like? So I'd rather just tweak the one problem thing to suit myself than throw it out entirely.

Like I could see moving some of the zone progression stuff to action-based matters, where instead of the stakes getting higher being based on time, maybe it's based more on if players make certain types of really big mistakes or bad moves or bad rolls/twists, so they then have a sense of "oops I broke something OK guys my bad we need to fix that" and then the increased zone stakes feels based on their own actual actions rather than on an impersonal ticking clock.

Point the First:

I didn't imply or state that the scene tracker was combat only.  Rather, I said it's used in Action Scenes, rather than Montage or Open-roleplay scenes.  An action scene likely encompasses a number of items that are not merely "Punch the bad guys till they fall down."  In one Action scene, one character may be overwatching a hallway with a pulse cannon, while another hacks the high-security lock, and a third works to cobble together a makeshift explosive.  Given that, I still think it's perfectly reasonable to provide players (and their characters) with active deadlines.  ("You've got 10 rounds to make it to the security override controls or you're going to be overwhelmed with Omnitron 7 drones…")

I do think that the false Tomb of Anubis utiilizes the GYRO tracker poorly, as the obstacles themselves are severely abstracted.  That said, I easily think that adventure is the weakest of the six, eschewing structure in order to achieve overall feel and concept neither of which were executed well in the text.

Point the Second:

My point wasn't a conflation between the GYRO scene tracker and individual player turns, but rather a holistic statement:  I like tension in my games.  I like to maintain a ticking clock (or bomb, as the case may be).  And, if the group doesn't act before the clock runs out, I as a GM am not going to mellow out on them, simply because they couldn't/didn't/wouldn't make a decision when pressed.  If you, as an individual, hem and haw during your turn (making others wait on you and otherwise slowing down the action), I move on without you.  

Your group may be different in that regard; that's great if it is.  For me, I like the idea of a big warning sign for the group saying, "You have 8 rounds to complete 3 objectives.  Get 'em done!"  On an individual level, that manifests as "Your character is surrounded by 3 goons and Citizen Blorp is dragging away the reporter by the hair–make a decision!"  At my table, he who hesitates is lost.

posts.cooked:
Jeysie, I feel that you like to put words in people’s mouths and twist statements to suit your interpretation of them. I never said I hate long, drawn out role-playing sessions. I am currently running a game that takes place entirely in a giant sandbox of a town and relies completely on the players choosing a direction or plot thread and going from there. (Want to see it? Go here: Deadlands: Golgatha) I don’t guide them at all, only react to their choices. Been running this game weekly for just over a year. In that time they have died several times, discovered weird stuff, met interesting NPCs, tried to catch a serial killer, fought horrors man was not meant to know, and actively blew up the entire town to smithereens. They have also spent a lot of time going to the store, hanging out in bars, negotiating the price of horses, keeping watch at night, and running away from things that aren’t dangerous. And they still haven’t discovered everything I put into the town yet. A year of playing and there are still places they haven’t seen, people they haven’t met, plots they haven’t picked up. The pace is completely dictated by them and we have a great time.

I do enjoy that kind of role-playing. Never said I didn’t. And I would appreciate it if maybe you didn’t attack me by making such assumptions about me or using language that reads like you are belittling me when all I’m doing is trying to be helpful here with regards to running a Sentinels RPG session from the Starter Kit.

Everyone has their play style that they like. If spending hours checking into a hotel and eating dinner is your idea of fun, by all means, do it. I’ve done similar sessions and they were extremely satisfying. So don’t think I’m saying it’s bad or that I hate it or draw conclusions that are entirely unrelated to the topic at hand.

We aren’t talking about an RPG here where the main idea is you play a day in the life of a superhero. This is an RPG about making an exciting line of comic book stories, set in a Silver Age era of comic book superheroes. In this context, readers reading an entire comic book about Tachyon going to dinner, and that’s all that happens, well, it seems like readers wouldn’t much like to read that comic. But a comic where Tachyon is faced with stopping a horde of spider bots and rescuing citizens and having a fellow superhero in peril… That’s more fitting with the excitement and drama of a Silver Age superhero comic book.

Ultimately the table is your group of writers, and if everyone thinks the Tachyon Goes To Dinner issue will excite their “readers”, then I say do it! It’s your game! There’s no one right way to have fun with it. Decades of running RPGs has taught me that.

I do think that action scenes in a Sentinels RPG session need to feel high stakes action that is worthy of the attention of a superhero, particularly since that seems to be the point of action scenes in the Sentinels RPG. Whereas montage scenes are the exposition, the all-roleplay downtime between the times when the city is in peril. One entire session of Sentinels RPG is supposed to be one comic book issue, so a montage scene that eats up all of one session should probably have some really juicy character development or plot advancement to be worthy of “publishing” so to speak.

There’s ways to work that kind of thing. Tachyon goes to a fancy restaurant expecting to meet with her wife, but then she gets there and finds herself sitting across from Friction, her nemesis! As Tachyon is about to speedster her enemy into submission, Friction flips a switch on a clock device she hid underneath the table. If Tachyon attempts to use any of her speedster abilities, the device will trigger and all the bombs in the restaurant will go off killing everyone before Tachyon can save them! But! If Tachyon can get through this dinner without creating a scene and just hears Friction out, then Friction will leave and all the bombs will be disarmed ten minutes after Friction exits the restaurant.

Now we have a montage scene that engages the superhero in role-play with stakes (steaks?) that makes it not an ordinary dinner scene. There’s a purpose to it, one that likely will lead to the next scene of action as Tachyon needs to disarm the bombs and catch Friction, or maybe Spite is hunting Friction for reasons and she wants Tachyon’s help, or maybe Friction knows that Biomancer is doing terrible things that involve replacing her, or any number of other comic book plot tropes that explains why Friction needs to have dinner with Tachyon. Maybe she just wants to have dinner with her. I don’t know. But it should be viewed through the lens of what would happen in a comic book; of what would engage a comic book reader.

That’s the experience that I think the Sentinels RPG is trying to provide. I’m not saying that other experiences are bad or that they’re wrong or that I hate them. I’m saying that the purpose of the game is to do what heroes do. Defend the weak and the innocent. Throw a wrench in the works when the villains set their plans in motion. Jump in and lend a hand when your teammates are in trouble. Stand up for your principles. Punch evil right in the face.

Save the day.

After all, that’s what it says right in the Gameplay Guide.

And if you think there’s no role-playing during an action scene, honey, you have no idea. There is a ton of role-playing. Especially in this system since you have to role-play it first, then put together the dice. In other systems it’s usually the other way around, where the rules tell you what to do and the role-play is secondary to the roll-play during combat.

posts.cooked:
PlatinumWarlock:

In one Action scene, one character may be overwatching a hallway with a pulse cannon, while another hacks the high-security lock, and a third works to cobble together a makeshift explosive.

Yeah, and it's like:

  1. You have to figure out that hacking a security lock is what needs to be done in the first place. (Step 1)

  2. You have to get together the materials to handle this. (Step 2)

  3. You have to actually do it. (Step 3)

  4. If it fails, you have to either repeat this all over again or come up with a Plan B.

This is totally fine in RP that's allowed to progress at a normal state of speed. That's not fine when you've got only a limited amount of turns to do things.

Same more or less with the explosive. Figuring out what you want to do. Getting together what you need to do it. Accounting for what happens if it doesn't work the first time.

PlatinumWarlock:

My point wasn't a conflation between the GYRO scene tracker and individual player turns, but rather a holistic statement:  I like tension in my games.

And I like tension in the form of tension that's sprung naturally from the actual roleplayed actions in the game. Not from the GM rushing us along at an artifical breakneck pace, because that's not exciting, it's stressful and un-fun.

PlatinumWarlock:

And, if the group doesn't act before the clock runs out, I as a GM am not going to mellow out on them, simply because they couldn't/didn't/wouldn't make a decision when pressed.

Why, though? Your job as GM is not to command the players to march to your beat against their will, it's to help them have fun and tell fun stories. I mean, the Sentinels RPG's own gameplay guide says this.

PlatinumWarlock:

If you, as an individual, hem and haw during your turn (making others wait on you and otherwise slowing down the action), I move on without you.  Your group may be different in that regard; that's great if it is.

Well, yeah, my group respects that the point of RPing is for everyone at the table to have fun, not for the GM alone to have fun while everyone else is stressed out and feels like they don't get to do anything fun.

Now I feel regretful in offering to RP with you, because while your ideas are interesting, your GM style is very very counterproductive to anyone getting to do any actual real roleplaying. As such, your great ideas would go to waste because everyone would be too busy racing through the plot at warp speed to ever let anyone properly do anything with them.

[quote="PlatinumWarlock"] If you, as an individual, hem and haw during your turn (making others wait on you and otherwise slowing down the action), I move on without you.  Your group may be different in that regard; that's great if it is. [/quote] Well, yeah, my group respects that the point of RPing is for everyone at the table to have fun, not for the GM alone to have fun while everyone else is stressed out and feels like they don't get to do anything fun. Now I feel regretful in offering to RP with you, because while your ideas are interesting, your GM style is very very counterproductive to anyone getting to do any actual real roleplaying. As such, your great ideas would go to waste because everyone would be too busy racing through the plot at warp speed to ever let anyone properly do anything with them.

posts.name: Jeysie
posts.cooked:
twoeyedjack:

Jeysie, I feel that you like to put words in people's mouths and twist statements to suit your interpretation of them.

Dude, t his started because YOU put words in MY mouth and twisted MY statements to suit YOUR interpretation of them. That is what actually happened here.

Because I said literally nothing initally except that my own group likes to take their time roleplaying and took a long time to get through combat, and you out of literally nowhere decided to give me a full page lecture on how you thought I was derailing the GM's plot or taking forever to choose what to do, even though literally absolutely nowhere did I actually say that.

So my response to you was trying my best to make any sense at all of why you even made that whole lecture to me to begin with, because it seemed to have literally NOTHING to do with anything I actually said!

So I would ask you to not make untrue accusations of me, especially when you're accusing me of things you yourself did to me. That's not fair or respectful of you to do to me.

twoeyedjack:

I never said I hate long, drawn out role-playing sessions.

Dude.

https://greaterthangames.com/comment/184425#comment-184425

twoeyedjack:

While you certainly could just give the players free reign to determine their objectives and their approach, it leads to long, drawn out sessions where the progress of the game is entirely in the hands of the players. Anyone with gamemaster experience knows how that will go; a lot of floundering around and putzing about until a bad guy is thrown in front of them, and then they punch the bad guy until it doesn't get up again, and they steal the bad guy's stuff.

Occasionally you'll have a group that can stay on task, but those seem to be the exception and not the norm.

Why did you right there criticize long, drawn out sessions, if you don't dislike long, drawn out sessions?

twoeyedjack:

And I would appreciate it if maybe you didn't attack me by making such assumptions about me

And I would appreciate it if you accepted the fact that it's not an attack for someone to disagree with you based on things you literally outright said (points above).

twoeyedjack:

In this context, readers reading an entire comic book about Tachyon going to dinner, and that's all that happens, well, it seems like readers wouldn't much like to read that comic.

I have had plenty of occasions where I've read issues of comics with superheroes doing day to day stuff and I've enjoyed them plenty because I like superheroes as characters in addition to their combat powers.

Go back through the Letters Page podcasts and listen for Liz C.; you'll notice I spend a lot of time asking stuff like what the characters do on their time off or how they relate to each other, because that's what I find interesting.

And more relevantly I have the same right to what I find fun to roleplay as you have the right to yours.

Nowhere in this post have I made ANY disparaging remarks towards the way OTHER people like to play. Even when I mentioned dungeon crawls aren't for me, I still said I appreciate that other people like them!

So why are you (and PlatinumWarlock) disparaging the way I or anyone else likes to roleplay? That's not respectful of me or other roleplayers.

twoeyedjack:

I do think that action scenes in a Sentinels RPG session need to feel high stakes action that is worthy of the attention of a superhero,

And that's great, but that just means you have the high stakes come naturally from what the players do during the session. Not from artifically rushing the players along in ways that are stressful instead of exciting.

twoeyedjack:

I'm not saying that other experiences are bad or that they're wrong or that I hate them.

Yeah, you are. You have spent this entire time insinuating strongly that you think the way I and others roleplay is objectively bad. It is disrespectful and I would like you (and PlatinumWarlock) to cease doing so.

twoeyedjack:

And if you think there's no role-playing during an action scene, honey, you have no idea.

OK, look, I also would like you to drop the disrespectful condescension too.

This is why I get upset and complain about the way people treat me. All I have done anywhere in this thread is politely and civilly explain why I feel the way I enjoy roleplaying would run into issues with this system, and have made what I tried to have be constructive suggestions as to how to fix my concerns without throwing out the entire system.  In return I've gotten you and PlatinumWarlock berating me for literally no good reason and accusing me of things I didn't do or say.

I would like to point out that browbeating me does not convince me to change my mind about my misgivings with this system. All it does is make me think I would never want to play with you or PlatinumWarlock as a GM because neither of you seem to have any respect for your players.

And I feel sad in PlatinumWarlock's case because he had great ideas, but I'd rather play with a GM who just runs average plots but wants to make sure their players are having fun, than a GM who has good ideas but is going to drag me along by my collar everyplace.
